issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes hypervigilance, startle, danger in silence, fragmented/avoided trauma memory, and appraisals of betrayal and injustice after police violence. Those other items describe a fearful, threat-sensitive presentation; endorsing active risk-taking as a core threat item pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported elsewhere in the selected nodes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself
issues.explanation: 'Can't Rely on Self' is a weaker fit than the other appraisals for this trauma/context. The profile is organized around external betrayal/injustice linked to police violence, but this item shifts to global self-distrust without corresponding self-blame, shame, incompetence, or strategy items elsewhere. In combination with the strong betrayal/injustice theme, it creates a less coherent appraisal profile.

vignette: Rafael's eyes still scan the room with a mix of habit and unease, a reflex honed from years of working as a parole officer in tough neighborhoods. But it wasn't the streets that had finally brought him to therapy - it was the memories he'd been trying to keep at bay since that fateful night five years ago, when his own colleagues turned on him during a routine arrest. The sounds of sirens and shouting still echo in Rafael's mind, but whenever he tries to recall the details, his thoughts are shrouded in an unsettling fog. He pushes the memories away before they can fully form, leaving him with only fragmented images: a baton raised high, the feeling of pavement scraping against his cheek, the weight of a knee on his chest. The more he tries to piece together what happened, the more it feels like a dream - or a nightmare - rather than reality. Rafael's been having trouble sleeping ever since. He wakes up with his heart racing, as if he's still running from those who were supposed to be his brothers in blue. Even during the day, when his own heartbeat pounds in his ears, Rafael feels like he's on high alert, waiting for the other shoe to drop. His wife has noticed it too - how he startles at every little noise, how he constantly scans their surroundings whenever they're out. The triggers are everywhere: a police car driving by, people arguing in public, even the sound of his own heartbeat. For Rafael, each one serves as a reminder that danger lurks around every corner, and that silence can be just as ominous as any shout. He's come to believe that if he'd only been more vigilant, more prepared, maybe things wouldn't have gone so horribly wrong. That sense of failure - or rather, the failure of those who were supposed to protect him - haunts Rafael still. The memory of being left for dead on that pavement, with no one to turn to but the system that had betrayed him, feels like an injustice he can hardly bear. He knows it's eating away at him, making him question his own judgment and trustworthiness as a parole officer. As Rafael recounts these memories in therapy, his voice cracks with emotion - not just from the pain of reliving those moments but also from the knowledge that nothing has been done to hold anyone accountable for what happened. He feels like he's still searching for justice, still seeking vindication for the wounds he received at the hands of those who were sworn to protect and serve. But even as Rafael talks about his desire for closure, his eyes betray a lingering fear - that he'll never be able to shake off the feeling of being on edge, waiting for the next shoe to drop. His wife's gentle touch or a calm conversation with friends might offer temporary respite, but deep down, Rafael knows that until he confronts the memories head-on and finds some measure of peace, he'll remain trapped in this endless cycle of threat and fear. As our sessions draw to a close for the day, Rafael looks around the room once more - not just scanning his surroundings out of habit but also searching for reassurance that he's taking the first steps toward healing. For now, it's a fragile hope, one that flickers like a candle flame in the wind. But with each passing moment, he knows he'll have to confront those memories again, and this time, face the darkness head-on.
